title: The long round of births
hookLine: the Granth speaks of many lives and the chance this human life is
last: DEEDS SHAPE THE ROBE; GRACE OPENS THE DOOR.

lines: A LINE IN THE EVENING PRAYER.
cards: In the evening, in homes and gurdwaras, Sikhs pray Rehras. Partway through comes a line that sounds less like a hymn than a tap on the shoulder.
In paraphrase: you have been given this human body; this is your turn to meet the Lord of the universe. Your turn. Like a number called at a counter after a long wait.
The line assumes a long line, a queue of lives before this one. It doesn't argue for it. It just turns, looks you in the eye, and says: now.

teach.h: THE ROUND: MANY LIVES, MANY FORMS.
teach.b: Behind the line is the long round. The Granth speaks of the soul passing through many lives and many forms: in some hymns, as a worm, a bird, a tree, a stone, round and round. It doesn't linger on the details.
The round is the background, the long road behind.

The hymn in Rehras is by Guru Arjan, and its point is the human life: the turn, the moment the door can open. Sikh teachers add that of all the forms in the round, this is the one that can remember the Name on purpose.
The same hymn says, in paraphrase: your other tasks are of no use here; join the company of the holy and dwell on the Name alone. That sounds stern, but it's about priority, not about quitting work.
The farmer still farms. The line asks what the farming is for. Why does this matter on a Tuesday?
If you believe in many lives, the line makes this one precious: don't waste the turn.

teach.h: TODAY IS PART OF THE TURN.
teach.b: If you don't, it still lands: this life is the one in your hands, and today is part of it. Either way, the Guru isn't trying to frighten anyone with the long round.
He's pointing at the counter where your number just came up.

how: Sikhs recite Rehras Sahib in the evening, which includes Guru Arjan's line that this human body is the turn to meet the Lord of the universe.

games.q: what does “the long round of births” mean?
o: a yearly festival held on a child's birthday
a prayer said in a circle at the end of the day
many lives and forms, with this human life as the turn

games.q: the long round: tap the pairs.
p: your turn to meet the Lord

s: the line about the human body as your turn is in Rehras
a hymn by Guru Arjan, prayed in the evening.
the hymn tells listeners to quit their work
it's about priority: what the work is for.
in the Granth, the human life is pictured as a chance
the turn when the door can open.

games.q: you've come through a long round of lives, and now you have a human body. what does Guru Arjan's hymn say this life is for?
o: gathering as much as possible before it ends.
meeting the Lord: remembering the Name.
resting, since the round will go on anyway.
games.why: this is your turn to meet the Lord of the universe, the hymn says; other tasks are of no use here.

practice: Feel your hands, your feet, the weight of your body on the seat: this body, this one, and today happening once. Let one thing come to mind you'd be sorry to leave undone, a call, a moment of attention, a word of thanks.
If you pray, offer the day as your turn; if not, sit with the plain fact that you're alive right now.

wordCard.voice: The long round of births. The Granth's picture of many lives and many forms, and the human life as the turn: the chance to meet the One. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: turn, time; in Rehras, this human body is your turn.

carryVoice: Your line: this life is the chance. Your number has come up, right here. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Ang 176 (Gauri, Guru Arjan: forms of the round)
